newsitem.title: GERMANY: No decisions at German tax commission meeting.
newsitem.headline: No decisions at German tax commission meeting.

text.p: Germany's coalition tax commission met on Wednesday to thrash out key points of a major tax reform to take effect in 1999, but put off announcing its final proposals until the new year.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who chairs the commission, said after the meeting -- supposed to have been its last -- that the policy group would get together four more times before presenting a final proposal at the end of January.
"I never said we would publish the main points (of the reform) this year," Waigel told reporters after the meeting.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's three-party alliance wants to make big income tax cuts in 1999 to boost Germany's economy and cut tax evasion, but has not yet agreed by how much.
Waigel has favoured cutting Germany's entry tax rate to around 20 percent from 26 percent, and reducing the top bracket to 40 percent from 53 percent.

The Free Democrats (FDP), junior coalition partners, want a three-band system with brackets at 15, 25 and 35 percent, but are firmly against a two-point increase in value-added tax which Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) want.
"I see no chance of a value-added tax increase -- at least not in this parliament," FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle told German Radio. Elections are due in 1998.

Delegates said Wednesday's talks skirted the issue of tax rates, although they said the consensus was moving towards phasing in a three-band income tax system to replace Germany's existing sliding scale system.
Waigel said progress had been made over dealing with corporation taxes and levies on earnings from interest, but he declined to give any details.
Earlier, he said most of the work had been done in scrapping a series of tax breaks to help offset the 100 billion marks in lost revenues likely to result from the tax shake-up.
The coalition will next week discuss demands by the FDP to cut the solidarity surcharge, a tax raised to finance east German reconstruction.
The FDP, which reluctantly agreed this autumn to postpone a reduction originally planned next year, wants to cut the surcharge by two points from the current 7.5 percent in 1998.
